div.p: 1. If you who preside over the Roman Empire are not permitted, in some open and lofty place, at the very summit of the state where you sit in judgment, to examine plainly and to weigh openly what truth there really is in the cause of the Christians; if in this single instance your authority is afraid or ashamed to inquire publicly with the diligence of justice; if, finally — as has lately happened — the persecution of this sect, too zealously pursued by the courts of private households, blocks its defence: then let truth be permitted to reach your ears, if only by the hidden path of a silent document.

Truth makes no appeal on its own behalf, for it does not wonder at its own condition. It knows that it lives as a stranger upon the earth, that among aliens it easily finds enemies, but that its lineage, its home, its hope, its favour, its dignity are in heaven. One thing for now it longs for: that it should not be condemned unheard.

1. If, in the end, it is certain that we are the most criminal of men, why are we treated by you otherwise than our equals — that is, the rest of the criminal — when the same treatment ought to attend the same offence?

Whatever others are charged with, when they are charged they use both their own voice and a hired advocate to commend their innocence. The opportunity to answer, to dispute, lies open, since it is not even lawful to condemn men wholly undefended and unheard.

They praise what they know, they blame what they do not know, and what they know they spoil with what they do not — though it were juster to prejudge the hidden by the manifest than to condemn beforehand the manifest by the hidden.

We will answer to each of the things we are said to commit in secret, the very things we find them committing openly; the things in respect of which we are reckoned wicked, vain, deserving of condemnation, deserving of mockery.

Tiberius, then, in whose time the Christian name entered the world, when tidings were brought to him from Syria Palestine of the things which there had revealed the truth of this divinity, laid the matter before the senate with the prerogative of his own vote in its favour. The senate, because it had not itself approved, rejected it; Caesar held to his opinion, threatening danger to the accusers of the Christians.

Whither have those laws gone that curbed extravagance and ambition — which ordered that no more than a hundred asses be spent upon a dinner, that no more than one hen be served, and that not a fattened one; which removed from the senate a patrician for possessing ten pounds of silver, as for a great mark of ambition; which straightway pulled down theatres springing up to the corruption of morals; which suffered the insignia of rank and noble birth to be assumed neither rashly nor with impunity?

From your own dissembling it is to be inferred that the thing is not what you do not dare even yourselves to unearth. A far different task you impose upon the executioner against the Christians — not that they should tell what they do, but that they should deny what they are.

Come, plunge the steel into an infant that is no one's enemy, guilty of nothing, the son of all; or, if that is another's office, do you only stand by a man that is dying before he has lived; await the fresh soul as it flees, catch the new-shed blood, glut your bread with it, eat freely.

Infants were sacrificed to Saturn in Africa, openly, down to the proconsulship of Tiberius, who exposed the very priests upon the trees of his temple — those trees that overshadowed their crimes — on votive crosses, the soldiery of our own country being witness, which performed that very office for that proconsul.

We have ceased to worship your gods from the time that we have recognized that they are not gods. This, then, you ought to require: that we prove that they are not gods, and therefore not to be worshipped, because they would deserve to be worshipped only if they were gods. And then Christians would deserve to be punished, if it were established that those whom they did not worship, because they thought them not to be gods, were in fact gods.

First of all, you must grant that there is some more sublime god, a certain master and dispenser of divinity, who made gods out of men. For neither could they have assumed to themselves a divinity which they did not possess, nor could any other bestow it upon those who lacked it, save one who properly possessed it.

As regards the images themselves, I find fault with nothing else than that their materials are sisters of common pots and vessels, or that, from those very pots and vessels, they change as it were their fate by consecration, the licence of art transfiguring them — and that most insultingly, and in the very making sacrilegiously; so that in truth it may be to us, above all, who are punished on account of these very gods, a consolation in our punishments that they themselves suffer the like in being made.

Consider whether I lie. First indeed, since you, some of you, worship some gods, others others, of course you offend those whom you do not worship. The preference of one cannot proceed without insult to another, since neither can choice be made without rejection.

But, turning to your literature, by which you are trained to prudence and the liberal duties, how many mockeries do I find! that the gods clashed in battle among themselves for the Trojans and the Achaeans, like matched pairs of gladiators; that Venus was wounded by a human arrow, because she wished to rescue her son Aeneas, all but slain by that same Diomedes;

The very scripts of the players portray all their foulness. The Sun mourns his son hurled from heaven, while you make merry; Cybele sighs for the disdainful shepherd, while you do not blush; you endure to have the records of Jupiter sung, and Juno, Venus, and Minerva judged by a shepherd.

For in the fifth book of his Histories, beginning the Jewish war from the origin of the nation, after arguing what he pleased both about that origin and about the name and religion of the nation, he relates that the Jews, when delivered out of Egypt — or, as he thought, driven out — in the vast and waterless wilds of Arabia, perishing with thirst, used as guides to a spring some wild asses which, after feeding, were thought to be seeking water; and that for this kindness they consecrated the figure of a like beast.

He is invisible, though he be seen; incomprehensible, though by grace he be represented; inestimable, though he be estimated by human senses. Therefore is he true and so great. For what can commonly be seen, comprehended, estimated, is less than the eyes by which it is grasped, and the hands by which it is contaminated, and the senses by which it is detected; but what is immeasurable is known only to itself.

For men worthy of him through the innocence of their righteousness, who knew God and could make him known, he sent forth from the beginning into the world, flooded with the divine Spirit, to proclaim that there is one only God, who founded the universe, who fashioned man from the clay (for this is the true Prometheus), who ordered the world by fixed dispositions and ends of time;

All substances therefore and all materials, the origins, the orders, the sources of every venerable writing of yours, most nations too and famous cities, and the hoary memorials of histories, and finally the very forms of letters, those marks and guardians of things — and (I think we are still saying too little) your very gods, I say, the very temples and oracles and rites — the casket of a single prophet outdoes by ages, in which is seen laid up the treasure of the whole Jewish covenant, and thence already of ours.

Whatever is now done was foretold; whatever is now seen was once heard. That the earth swallows cities, that the seas defraud men of islands, that wars without and within tear nations asunder, that kingdoms clash with kingdoms, that famine and pestilence and local calamities and frequent mortalities lay waste, that the lowly are exchanged for the lofty and the lofty for the lowly,

or because, apart from the matter of age, we have nothing to do with the Jews — neither as regards the restrictions of diet, nor the solemnities of days, nor the very seal upon the body, nor the fellowship of the name — which surely ought to be the case if we were bound to the same God.

All the poets know them; even the unlearned crowd uses them often as a curse. For they pronounce Satan too, the prince of this evil race, with the same voice of execration, out of the soul's own consciousness. Angels too even Plato did not deny.

Or if angels and demons work the same things that your gods do, where then is the pre-eminence of divinity, which surely must be believed superior to every power? Will it not then be more worthily presumed that these are the very ones who make themselves gods, since they do the same things that make gods to be believed, than that gods are the equals of angels and demons?

But, on the contrary, the reproach has rebounded upon you, who, worshipping falsehood, not only by neglecting but by openly assailing the true religion of the true God, commit against the truth the real crime of true irreligion.

Yet, since the mention of the Roman name in particular has come up, I will not omit the encounter to which that presumption invites — of those who say that the Romans, for the desert of their most diligent religiosity, have been raised to such a height of greatness as to have seized the world, and that the gods are so truly gods that those flourish beyond the rest who do their service beyond the rest.

Why do you go astray? Earlier than some of its own gods is the woodland Rome; she reigned before she built so great a circuit of the Capitol. The Babylonians had reigned before the Pontiffs, and the Medes before the Quindecimviri, and the Egyptians before the Salii, and the Assyrians before the Luperci, and the Amazons before the Vestal virgins.
But some think it madness, that, when we might both sacrifice for the moment and depart unharmed, keeping our purpose in our mind, we prefer obstinacy to safety.

We have come, then, to the second charge, of treason against a more august majesty, since with greater dread and a more crafty timidity you watch over Caesar than over Olympian Jupiter himself. And rightly, if you knew it. For who of the living, whoever he be, is not more powerful than any dead man?

For surely they would first protect their own statues and images and temples, which, as I suppose, the soldiers of the Caesars keep safe by their watches. Nay, I think these very materials come from the metals of the Caesars, and whole temples stand by the nod of Caesar.

They reflect how far the powers of their empire avail, and so they understand God; against whom they cannot prevail, by him they recognize that they prevail. Let the emperor make war on heaven; let him lead heaven captive in his triumph; let him set watches over heaven, lay tributes on heaven. He cannot.

Know from them that it is enjoined upon us, to the overflowing of kindness, to pray to God even for our enemies, and to invoke good upon our persecutors. Who are more the enemies and persecutors of Christians than those on whose majesty we are arraigned for treason?

But we swear too — not, indeed, by the genii of the Caesars, but by their welfare, which is more august than all genii. Do you not know that genii are called demons, and thence, by a diminutive word, demonia? We look up to the judgment of God in the emperors, who has set them over the nations.

And therefore, as more my own, I do more for his welfare; since I not only ask it of him who can grant it, or ask it as one who deserves to obtain it, but also, in that I keep the majesty of Caesar below God, I the more commend him to God, to whom alone I subject him. But I subject him to one to whom I do not make him equal.

He who is father of his country — how is he its lord? But the name of affection is also more welcome than that of power. Even in a household men are called fathers rather than lords. So far is it from being right that the emperor should be called God, a thing that cannot be believed without not only the most shameful but even a pernicious flattery.

A great service, no doubt, to bring out braziers and couches into the public street, to feast from street to street, to make the city wear the look of a tavern, to work mud out of wine, to run in troops to insults, to indecencies, to the enticements of lust! Is public joy thus expressed by public disgrace? Do those things befit the festal days of princes which befit no other days?

So far is it true that the piety and religion and faith owed to emperors does not consist in offices of this kind, by which hostility too can the rather perform its part as a veil for itself, but in those morals by which divinity commands that loyalty be shown as truly toward all men as it must of necessity be shown toward emperors.

For of this take note among yourselves. How often do you rage savagely against the Christians, partly out of your own minds, partly in obedience to the laws? How often too, even without regard to you, the hostile rabble assails us of its own right with stones and fires? With the very frenzies of the Bacchanals they do not spare even the dead Christians, but tear them from the rest of the tomb, from the asylum, as it were, of death, mangle and rend them in pieces, now no longer whole, now no longer themselves.

For, unless I am mistaken, the cause for forbidding associations rests upon a provident care for public order, lest the city be torn into factions — a thing which might easily disturb the assemblies, the councils, the senate-houses, the gatherings, even the public shows, by the clashing emulation of rival enthusiasms, especially now that men had begun to make their violence a thing of profit, venal and for hire.

We meet together in an assembly and congregation, that, as it were with marshalled forces, we may besiege God with our prayers. This violence is pleasing to God. We pray too for the emperors, for their ministers and the powers, for the state of the world, for the quiet of affairs, for the delay of the end.

If the Tiber rises to the walls, if the Nile does not rise to the fields, if the sky has stood still, if the earth has moved, if there is famine, if there is plague — at once the cry is "The Christians to the lion!" So many to a single one?

"This," you say, "may be turned back upon your God too, if he likewise suffers his own worshippers also to be harmed for the sake of the profane." Admit first his dispensations, and you will not turn it back.

We remember that we owe thanks to God, our Lord and Creator; we reject no fruit of his works; we only temper ourselves, lest we use them beyond measure or amiss. And so it is not without your forum, not without your meat-market, not without your baths, shops, workshops, inns, market-days, and the rest of your commerce, that we dwell together with you in this world.

To be unprofitable to these is a great profit. And yet, whatever loss your interest suffers through this sect, it can be balanced by some protection. How highly do you value — I will not now say those who cast out demons from you, I will not now say those who offer up prayers for you too to the true God, because perhaps you do not believe it — but those from whom you can have nothing to fear?

For now we call your own acts to witness — you who daily preside over the judging of prisoners, who discharge accusations by your sentences. So many guilty are reckoned up by you under the various headings of their crimes: which of them there is set down as an assassin, a cutpurse, a temple-robber, a seducer, a robber of bathers — which of them is also entered as a Christian? Or when Christians are brought forward under their own title, which of them is also such as those so many guilty?

But to you human estimation handed down innocence, and human dominion likewise enjoined it; hence yours is a discipline neither full nor so much to be feared, as touching the truth of innocence. As great is man's wisdom for pointing out the good as his authority for exacting it: the one as easy to be deceived as the other to be despised.

But while our truth is being made manifest to each, meanwhile unbelief — while it is convinced of the goodness of this sect, which is now known by use and intercourse — does not, indeed, reckon it a divine business, but rather a kind of philosophy. "The same things," it says, "the philosophers too counsel and profess — innocence, justice, patience, sobriety, chastity."

What poet, what sophist, who has not at all drunk from the fountain of the prophets? Thence, then, the philosophers slaked the thirst of their genius; so that, in what they have of ours, they liken us to themselves. Hence too, I suppose, philosophy was even cast out by certain peoples — by the Thebans, I mean, and by the Spartans and the Argives —

If by any law souls are made to pass back into bodies, why should they not return into the same substance, since this is what it means to be restored — to be that which one was? They are no longer the same as they were, since they could not have been what they were not, unless they ceased to be what they had been.

Grant now that the things we maintain are false, and deservedly presumption; yet they are necessary: inept, yet useful; since those who believe them are constrained to become better, for fear of an eternal punishment and in hope of an eternal refreshment. It is not therefore expedient to call false, nor to hold inept, things which it is expedient to presume true. On no ground is it lawful at all to condemn things that do good.

Yet a man both fights with all his might, and, winning in the battle, rejoices in the battle, though he had complained of the battle, because he gains both glory and spoil. It is a battle for us when we are summoned to your tribunals, that there, at the hazard of our life, we may contend for the truth. But the victory is to obtain that for which you contended. That victory has both the glory of pleasing God and the spoil of living forever.

What does the law lose here, ruling as it does in its own realm, if it grants a hearing? Will its power glory the more in this, that it condemns truth even after hearing it? But if it condemns truth unheard, then besides the odium of injustice it will earn the suspicion of some guilty conscience, in refusing to hear what, once heard, it could not condemn.

But to Christians alone nothing is permitted to be said that might clear the case, that might defend the truth, that might keep the judge from being unjust. One thing only is awaited, the thing that public hatred requires: the confession of the name, not the examination of a crime.

1. What of this — that most men so blindly strike at the hatred of this name that, even while bearing good witness to someone, they mix in a reproach of the name? "A good man is Gaius Seius, only that he is a Christian." Likewise another: "I am astonished that Lucius Titius, a wise man, has suddenly become a Christian." No one reflects whether Gaius is not good and Lucius prudent because they are Christians, or Christians because they are prudent and good.

Others, men whom before this name they had known as vagabonds, worthless, depraved, brand them by the very thing they praise. In the blindness of their hatred they stumble into approval: "What a woman! how wanton, how gay!" "What a youth! how dissolute, how amorous! They have become Christians!" So the name is set down to the account of reform.

But since, when our truth meets every charge, the authority of the laws is at last set up against it — so that either it is said that nothing can be reconsidered once the laws have spoken, or the necessity of obedience is, however reluctantly, preferred to truth — I will first join issue with you about the laws, as with the guardians of the laws.

Consult your records: there you will find that Nero was the first to rage with the imperial sword against this sect, just as it was rising at Rome. But in such a man as the consecrator of our condemnation we even glory. For whoever knows him can understand that nothing but some great good could have been condemned by Nero.

For I see dinners now to be reckoned at a hundred thousand sesterces; and silver mines wrought into dishes — too little to say of senators, when it is even of freedmen, or of men whose backs still feel the lash. I see theatres, and not single ones nor uncovered ones either; for, lest impure pleasure should grow cold even in winter, the Lacedaemonians were the first to devise the cloak for the games. I see no distinction of dress left between matrons and harlots.

The origin of this discipline, as we have already declared, is from Tiberius. With hatred of itself truth began. As soon as it appeared, it was an enemy. It has as many enemies as it has strangers — and properly, out of rivalry, the Jews; out of extortion, the soldiers; by very nature, even our own households.

Meanwhile, as you recline, reckon up the places — where the mother is, where the sister; mark them diligently, so that, when the darkness falls at the dogs' overturning of the lamps, you may not go astray. For you will have committed a sin, unless you have committed incest.
But even now this holy crime is carried on in secret. It is not Christians alone whom your gods despise; nor is any crime forever rooted out, nor does any god change his ways.

"But to us," you say, "they are gods." We appeal, and we make our appeal from you to your own conscience. Let that conscience judge us, let that condemn us, if it can deny that all these gods of yours were men.

But if there were no one to make gods, you presume in vain that gods were made, taking away the maker. Certainly, if they could have made themselves, they would never have been men, possessing, as they would, the power of a better condition.
You set Christians upon crosses and stakes. What image is there that the clay does not first shape upon a cross and a stake? It is on a gibbet that the body of your god is first dedicated.

You therefore already despise those whom you reject, whom in rejecting you do not fear to offend. For, as we touched on above, the standing of each god hung upon the estimation of the senate. He was no god whom a man, being consulted, refused, and in refusing condemned.

that Mars was nearly worn out by thirteen months in chains; that Jupiter, lest he should suffer the same violence from the other heaven-dwellers, was set free by the work of a certain monster; and now weeping the fall of Sarpedon, now foully lusting after his sister, with mention of mistresses formerly not so dearly loved.

The very fact that the likeness of your god clothes an ignominious and infamous head, that an impure body, bred for that art by effeminacy, represents some Minerva or Hercules — is not majesty violated and divinity outraged, while you applaud?

And from this, I suppose, it was presumed that we too, as near akin to the Jewish religion, are initiated to the same image. But that same Cornelius Tacitus — that most talkative of liars, to be sure — in the same history relates that Gnaeus Pompey, when he had taken Jerusalem and therefore entered the temple to spy out the secrets of the Jewish religion, found there no image at all.

This it is which makes God to be estimated, while he cannot be estimated. Thus the force of his greatness sets him before men both as known and as unknown. And this is the height of the offence of those unwilling to recognize him whom they cannot but know.

and thereafter what signs of his majesty in judgment he has put forth through rains, through fires; what disciplines he has determined for winning his favour; what rewards he has appointed for those who ignore, desert, and observe them; how, when this present age is brought to a close, he is to judge his worshippers unto the reward of eternal life, and the profane unto a fire likewise perpetual and unceasing — all who were dead from the beginning being raised and reshaped and reviewed, for the rendering of either desert.

If you have heard meanwhile of one Moses, he is of equal age with the Argive Inachus. By nearly four hundred years — for it is seven less — he comes before Danaus, himself the most ancient among you; he precedes the fall of Priam by about a thousand years; I might even say by five hundred more, that he precedes Homer too, having those whom I may follow.

that justice grows rare and iniquity grows rife, that care for all good disciplines grows numb, that even the offices of the seasons and the services of the elements swerve from their course, that the order of nature is disturbed by monsters and portents — all this was providently written. While we suffer it, it is read; while we recognize it, it is proved. A fit testimony to divinity, I think, is the truth of divination.

But the common people too now know Christ as some man, such as the Jews judged him, so that one may the more readily think us worshippers of a man. Yet we are not ashamed of Christ, since it is a joy to be reckoned and condemned under his name; nor do we hold any other opinion of God. It is necessary, therefore, to say a few things about Christ as God.

Witnesses to either name even the magicians are at hand. But how, out of certain angels corrupted of their own will, a yet more corrupt race of demons came forth, condemned by God along with the authors of the race and with him whom we have called their prince — the order of it is learned in the holy writings.

The difference of place distinguishes them, I suppose, so that you reckon those gods from their temples whom elsewhere you do not call gods; so that he who flies over sacred towers seems to rave in one way, he who leaps across his neighbours' roofs in another; and one power is pronounced in the man who gashes his genitals or his arms, another in him who cuts his own throat. The outcome of the frenzy is the same, and the reason of the instigation is one.

Now, even granting that they are gods, do you not admit, by the common estimation, that there is someone more sublime and more powerful, as it were the prince of the world, of perfect power and majesty? For most men so dispose divinity, that they will have the sovereignty of supreme dominion to be in the hands of one, his offices in the hands of many; as Plato describes the great Jupiter in heaven, attended by an army of gods and demons alike.

This reward, no doubt, has been paid out by the Roman gods in gratitude. Sterculus and Mutunus and Larentina advanced the empire! For I would not think that foreign gods would have wished to favour an alien nation more than their own, and to give to men beyond the sea their native soil, in which they were born, grew up, ennobled, and buried.

Finally, if Roman religions bestow kingdoms, never in time past would Judea have reigned — Judea, despiser of these common divinities, whose God you Romans honoured for a time with victims, and his temple with gifts, and his nation with treaties — never to have mastered it, had she not at the last sinned against Christ.

You give us advice, of course, by which we should cheat you; but we know whence such things are suggested, who sets all this in motion, and how, now by the cunning of persuasion, now by the harshness of cruelty, it works to cast down our steadfastness.

But you do not do this by reason rather than by regard for present power: so that in this too you will be caught being irreligious toward your own gods, since you assign more fear to human dominion. In short, among you men more readily swear falsely by all the gods than by the single genius of Caesar.

In short, many gods have had Caesar for an enemy. It tells for our case, if also for a friend, when he confers on them some bounty or privilege. How then shall those who are in Caesar's power, and wholly his, have Caesar's welfare in their power, so that they may seem able to bestow that which they themselves more easily obtain from Caesar?

He is great for this reason, that he is less than heaven. For he himself is his whose is both heaven and every creature. He is emperor from him from whom he was a man before he was emperor; from him is his power, from whom is also his breath.

But even by name and expressly: "Pray," he says, "for kings and for princes and powers, that all may be peaceful for you." For when the empire is shaken, and its other members too are shaken, surely we also, though we be reckoned strangers to the crowds, are found in some place of the calamity.

We know to be in them that which God has willed; and therefore we wish that to be safe which God has willed, and we hold this for a great oath. But demons — that is, genii — we are accustomed to adjure, in order to drive them out of men, not to swear by them, so as to confer on them the honour of divinity.

For I will not call the emperor God — either because I do not know how to lie, or because I do not dare to mock him, or because not even he himself will wish to be called God. If he is a man, it is the interest of a man to yield to God. Let him be content to be called emperor. That too is a great name, which is handed down by God. He who calls him God denies that he is emperor; unless he be a man, he is not emperor.

As if, having one emperor, you should call another by that name — would you not contract the greatest and most implacable offence of the one whom you have, an offence to be feared even by the very man whom you so called? Be religious toward God, you who would have him propitious to the emperor. Cease to believe another to be God, and so to call him God who has need of God.
Shall those who keep observance out of regard for Caesar, desert it for Caesar's sake; and shall licence in evil morals be piety, and the occasion of luxury be reckoned religion?

For these works of a good mind are not owed by us to emperors alone. We perform no good under exception of persons, because we do it for ourselves, who look for no payment of praise or reward from man, but from God, the exactor and rewarder of an impartial benevolence.

Yet what, from men so banded together, so resolved even to death for their wrong, has ever been requited in return — when even one night, with a few little torches, could work an abundance of vengeance, if among us it were lawful to pay back evil with evil? But far be it that a divine sect should avenge itself by human fire, or grieve to suffer that in which it is proved.

But for us, who are cold to all ardour of glory and dignity, there is no need of combination; nor is anything more foreign to us than public affairs. We acknowledge one commonwealth of all: the world.

We come together for the recollection of the divine writings, if the character of the present times compels us either to forewarn or to recall anything. At all events, we feed our faith with the holy words, we lift up our hope, we fix our confidence, and none the less we make firm our discipline by the inculcation of the precepts. There too are exhortations, chastisements, and the divine censure.

I ask you, before Tiberius — that is, before the coming of Christ — how many disasters fell upon the world and the cities? We read that Hiera, Anaphe, Delos, Rhodes, and Cos, islands, perished with many thousands of men.

For he who has once for all appointed an eternal judgment after the end of the age does not hasten the separation, which is the condition of judgment, before the end of the age. He is meanwhile impartial over the whole human race, both indulgent and rebuking. He has willed both prosperity to be common to the profane and adversity to his own, that by an equal fellowship we might all experience both his leniency and his severity.

We sail too with you, and serve in the army, and till the ground, and trade; and besides we share our skills, and make our works public for your use. How we can seem unprofitable to your business, with whom and from whom we live, I do not know.

With your own people the prison is always seething; with your own the mines are always sighing; with your own the beasts are always fattened; from among your own the producers of the shows always feed their droves of criminals. No one there is a Christian, unless he is plainly only that; or if he is something else too, he is no longer a Christian.

And so, which is fuller — to say, "You shall not kill," or to teach, "You shall not even be angry"? Which is more perfect — to forbid adultery, or to keep men even from the solitary lust of the eyes? Which is more learned — to forbid evil-doing, or evil-speaking too? Which more thorough — not to permit injury, or not to suffer even the requital of injury?

Why then are we, who are likened to them in discipline, not made equal to them in the licence and impunity of that discipline? Or why are not they too, as our equals, pressed to the offices which we, in not performing, are imperilled?

while they aim at our things, and, being men greedy of glory, as we have said, and given over to mere eloquence, if they stumbled upon anything in the holy Scriptures, after the manner of their own curiosity they turned it to their own works; neither believing them sufficiently to be divine, that they might forbear to interpolate them, nor sufficiently understanding them, as being even then still half-veiled, obscured even to the Jews themselves, whose property they seemed to be.

There would even be need, in many places, of leisure for the work, if we wished to sport in this matter — who might be seen reformed into what beast. But it is rather for our own defence, since we maintain that it is far more worthy of belief that man shall return from man, any man for any other, provided it be man; so that the same quality of soul may be restored into the same condition, even if not into the same shape.

1. If we are bidden, as we have said above, to love our enemies, whom have we to hate? Likewise, if, when wronged, we are forbidden to return the like, lest by the deed we become their equals, whom can we injure?

1. Ought not, then, this sect to be reckoned, with a little more leniency, among the lawful associations, seeing that nothing of the kind is committed by it which is wont to be feared from unlawful associations?

1. I will now myself set forth the doings of the Christian society, so that, having refuted the evil, I may show the good. We are a body knit together by the consciousness of our religion, by the unity of our discipline, by the bond of our hope.

1. On the contrary, the name of faction is to be applied to those who conspire in hatred of the good and the upright, who clamour against the blood of the innocent, alleging in defence of their hatred that empty plea too, that they think the Christians the cause of every public calamity, of every misfortune of the people.

1. You, then, are the troublers of human affairs, you the lure that ever draws on the public misfortunes — among whom God is spurned and statues are adored. For it ought to be held more credible that he is angry who is neglected than those who are worshipped; or else those gods are most unjust, if for the sake of the Christians they harm even their own worshippers, whom they ought to set apart from the deserts of the Christians.

1. But under another head of injuries too we are arraigned, and are said to be unprofitable in business. How so — men who live among you, of the same food, dress, furniture, of the same necessity for life? For we are not Brahmans, nor gymnosophists of the Indians, dwellers in the woods and exiles from life.

1. I will frankly confess who they are, if any, who could perhaps truly complain of the unprofitableness of Christians. The first will be pimps, panders, and procurers' touts; then assassins, poisoners, magicians; likewise soothsayers, diviners, and astrologers.
1. But indeed that loss to the commonwealth, as great as it is real, no one regards; that injury to the state no one weighs, when so many just men are spent, when so many innocent are made away with.

1. We alone, then, are innocent. What wonder, if it must be so? For indeed it must. Innocence taught us by God, we both know perfectly, as revealed by a perfect Master, and we faithfully keep, as commanded by an Inspector not to be despised.

1. We have taken our stand, as I think, against the whole indictment of crimes which demands the blood of the Christians. We have shown our whole condition, and by what means we can prove it to be such as we have shown — namely, by the trustworthiness and the antiquity of the divine writings, and likewise by the confession of the spiritual powers. Who will dare to refute us — not by craft of words, but by the same method by which we established our proof — concerning the truth?

1. Truth is more ancient than all things, unless I am mistaken; and this too serves me — the antiquity already established of the divine literature — that it may readily be believed it has been a treasury for every later wisdom. And were I not now sparing the bulk of my volume, I would run out into this proof too.

1. Come now, if some philosopher affirm — as Laberius does, after the opinion of Pythagoras — that a man is made out of a mule, a snake out of a woman, and bend all the arguments of his eloquence to that opinion by the power of his rhetoric, will he not move assent and fix belief, so that men should abstain even from animals for that reason? Should anyone hold the persuasion, lest perchance in his beef he should be eating some great-grandfather of his? But if a Christian promise that a man shall return from a man, the very Gaius come back as Gaius, he will be driven off by the people with stones rather than even with gatherings of approval.

1. These are the things which in us alone are called presumptions; in the philosophers and poets, the height of knowledge and signal genius. They are prudent, we are inept; they are to be honoured, we to be derided — nay, the rather even to be punished.

1. "Why then," you say, "do you complain that we persecute you, if you wish to suffer, since you ought to love those through whom you suffer what you wish?" Plainly we wish to suffer, but in the manner in which a soldier wishes for war. No one indeed suffers willingly, since suffering means both fear and peril.
